name: A Plain SDK Loop
question: Do I need a framework at all?
summary: An agent is a loop: call the model with tools, run the tools it asks for, send back the results, stop when it answers. With a provider SDK that is about 45 lines, with nothing hidden and no framework to upgrade. You then own everything else: retries, saving state, pausing for approval and resuming, tracing, streaming and parallel tool calls. Many production agents stay this simple; start here and adopt a framework when a specific need appears.
useCases: Simple agents with a few tools
Teams that want full control and few dependencies

items.detail: call, run tools, append results, repeat
a step limit so it cannot loop forever
saving and resuming, if runs are long
your own adapter if you change provider

steps: Write the loop with a step budget
Add persistence and tracing only when needed
pitfalls: Rebuilding a framework badly, one feature at a time
Blocking a web request while waiting for a human
remember: Start with the loop; adopt a framework for a need, not a trend.

steps.title: Describe the tools
steps.text: Two tools with JSON schemas: look up a transaction by UTR, and raise a dispute. Good descriptions matter more than any framework (Panel 8).

steps.title: Call the model inside a budget
steps.text: The loop sends the conversation and the tools. The step budget stops a confused agent from looping forever.

steps.title: Run the tools it asks for
steps.text: If the model stopped to use tools, run them and send back the results; otherwise its text is the answer. That is the whole agent.

steps.title: Gate the risky tool
steps.text: A person approves before a dispute is raised. In a plain loop this blocks; that is fine for minutes, not for days.

steps.title: Fail loudly
steps.text: If the budget runs out, raise an error rather than returning half an answer.

steps.title: Know what you now own
steps.text: About 30 lines, no framework to upgrade. Persistence, resume, tracing, streaming and parallel calls are yours to write if you need them.

pros: Nothing hidden: the loop is yours to read
No framework upgrades or breaking changes
Works in any language with an SDK
Easiest to debug and to explain to reviewers
cons: You write persistence, resume and tracing yourself
Approvals that take hours need extra work
Provider switching needs your own adapter
avoidWhen: Long-running cases with human approvals and crash recovery
Teams that would rebuild a framework badly

practice.scenario: Kosha Pay, a fictional UPI app, built its first dispute agent as a 45-line loop on a provider SDK: look up the transaction, and if money was debited but the payment failed, raise a dispute after a human approves. It ran in production for six months with nothing but a step budget, an approval gate and tracing. When cases began needing multi-day approvals, the team moved that one workflow to a durable framework and kept the simple agents as plain loops.

industries.use: Dispute and refund assistants with two or three tools
Order-status helpers that call one internal API

practice.analogy: Cooking at home before buying a restaurant kitchen: you learn exactly what the dish needs, and you buy equipment only for the steps that hurt.

practice.note: The approval here blocks the loop; for approvals that take hours, persist the state and resume later, or use a durable framework.

numericDrill.question: A plain agent loop is 30 lines. Later you add retries (about 40 lines), saving and restoring state (about 150), pausing for approval and resuming (about 120) and tracing (about 60). How many lines do you now maintain?
numericDrill.answer: 30 + 40 + 150 + 120 + 60 = 400 lines, most of them the durability features a framework such as LangGraph or Pydantic AI with Temporal provides. That is the signal to adopt one for this agent, not before.

interview.question: When would you not use an agent framework?
interview.answer: When the agent is a simple tool loop with a few tools, short runs and no need to pause and resume. A provider SDK loop is small, transparent and has no framework upgrades to track. Adopt a framework when a concrete need appears, such as durable state, human approvals that take hours, or multi-agent orchestration.

interview.question: What must a hand-written loop always have?
interview.answer: A step budget so it cannot run forever, clear tool schemas, error handling that returns failures to the model rather than crashing, an approval gate before risky actions, and tracing so you can see what happened.

mistakes.mistake: Adopting a framework for a two-tool agent
mistakes.fix: Start with the loop; add a framework for a real need
Adopt durable execution when runs get long

quiz.question: An approval takes two days. What is the problem with blocking inside a plain loop?
options: The process must stay alive and nothing survives a restart

quiz.question: Which guide argues that simple, composable patterns often beat complex frameworks?

options: It may be time to adopt a framework for those features

quiz.question: How do you switch providers in a plain loop?

options: Return the error to the model as a tool result

quiz.question: Where should an approval gate sit?
quiz.explanation: Gate the action, not the text.
